description: Lawyers are trained to be careful on the record and are bound by privilege. Ask about process, judgment, and the profession rather than about matters, and they open up considerably.

questions.text: How much of your work is arguing, and how much is predicting what the other side will do?
questions.lands_because: Corrects the courtroom-drama frame from inside. Most legal work is anticipation and risk allocation, and lawyers appreciate an interviewer who already suspects that.
followups: When did you get good at the predicting part?

questions.text: What do you know about a case in the first meeting that the client does not want to hear yet?
questions.lands_because: Early case assessment is a real skill, and the tension between honest evaluation and client management is the daily texture of practice.
followups: How do you eventually tell them?

questions.text: What does the billable hour do to how you work?
questions.lands_because: The central economic distortion of private practice, felt by everyone in it, and rarely discussed with an outsider who understands it is a structural question rather than an accusation.
followups: Have you worked under a different model? Was it better?
questions.avoid_if: The guest is a public defender, judge, or in-house counsel - use a workload or caseload question instead.

questions.text: What is the most common misconception your clients arrive with about how the law works?
questions.lands_because: Easy, generous, and it lets the guest be useful to the audience. Also surfaces the gap between legal reality and public understanding, which is the point of the episode.
followups: Where does that idea come from?

questions.text: Where is the line between zealous advocacy and something you would not do?
questions.lands_because: Uses the profession's own language, which signals you know the duty is real and not a loophole. That framing gets a considered answer instead of a defensive one.
followups: Have you watched someone cross it?

questions.text: What does the system do well that critics miss, and what do the critics get right?
questions.lands_because: The two-sided structure lets a lawyer defend the institution and criticize it in the same answer, which is where their actual view usually lives.
followups: What reform would you actually support?
